written.q: Describe how the colourisation assignment frames the problem in the Lab colour space, including the shapes of the input and target.
written.a: Lab splits colour into L (lightness, the grayscale picture) and a, b (colour). The network input is L with shape 1×128×128; the target is a and b with shape 2×128×128. Predict a and b, combine with L and convert Lab to RGB. Training images are resized to 128×128, converted RGB→Lab and scaled (L/50 − 1, ab/128); the same scaling is reversed when rebuilding the colour image.

written.q: Explain the U-Net used in the assignment: encoder, bottleneck, decoder, skip connections and output layer, with the shapes.
written.a: Encoder: DoubleConv blocks with 64, 128, 256, 512 channels, with max-pooling halving the size (128, 64, 32, 16). Bottleneck: 1024 channels at 8×8. Decoder: ConvTranspose2d doubles the size and halves channels, then the matching encoder output is concatenated (skip connection, so a block takes 512 + 512 = 1024 channels) and a DoubleConv follows, returning to 64 channels at 128×128. Output: 1×1 convolution to 2 channels with tanh, shape 2×128×128. Skip connections carry fine detail so the output lines up with the input.

written.q: Describe the training procedure and loss for the colouriser and how you would apply it to an old black-and-white photograph.
written.a: MSE between predicted and true a, b, optimised with Adam (lr 0.001) for 15–20 epochs (18 used); for each batch zero gradients, forward pass, MSE, backward (backpropagation), optimiser step; save a checkpoint each epoch and plot the loss. For a photo: convert to grayscale, resize to 128×128, use as L (scaled), predict a and b, recombine with L, convert to RGB and show the grayscale input, the prediction and the restored colour image.

written.q: Give two limits of this colouriser.
written.a: One grayscale image can match several plausible colourings (a jacket could be red or blue), so the output is plausible rather than true; MSE averages uncertain colours so results look muted. Also the training images are tiny CIFAR-10 pictures, so unusual scenes such as old portraits are harder.

written.q: (Background) Explain in your own words how a diffusion model generates an image.
written.a: Forward process: add a little random noise to real images again and again until only noise remains. Training: a neural network (often a U-Net) learns to predict the noise in a noisy image (MSE on the noise). Generation: start from pure random noise and repeatedly apply the network to remove a little noise each step until a clean new image appears; a text prompt can guide the steps (Stable Diffusion).

written.q: (Background) Compare GANs and VAEs as image generators.
written.a: GAN: a generator turns random numbers into fake images and a discriminator tries to tell real from fake; they compete and both improve, giving sharp images but hard training. VAE: an autoencoder whose encoder describes an image as a random latent cloud; generation samples a new point and decodes it; stable but often blurry.
